newsitem.title: Yugoslavia: Milosevic coalition expected to win Yugo polls.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic coalition expected to win Yugo polls.

text.p: Yugoslavia held its first elections on Sunday since the end of a four-year Balkan war amid forecasts Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic would lead his coalition to victory against opposition parties.
Authorities reported a low 29 percent turnout by midday for the federal and municipal elections, the state Tanjug news agency reported.
Polling stations opened at 7 a.m. (0600 GMT) and were due to close at 8 p.m. (1900 GMT) in Serbia and Montenegro, the two remaining Yugoslav republics.
Milosevic, blamed by the West for plunging old Yugoslavia into conflict, now presents himself as peacemaker.
His ruling alliance of the Socialist party and two other parties made no mention of the wars in Bosnia and Croatia during the campaign.
"I am certain the elections are of great significance for the stability of the whole region," he told reporters after voting in Belgrade.
Milosevic was accompanied by his wife, Mirjana Markovic, a Marxist who heads one of three parties backing the president.
A low voter turnout would be bad news for the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition, as Milosevic's parties rely on a loyal minority -- many of them pensioners -- with disciplined voting habits.
The opposition accused the authorities of preventing or discouraging their representatives from serving on some local electoral commissions, which supervise voting procedures.
In the capital Belgrade, the opposition alleged that in some cases electoral commissions were not given a chance to verify ballot results for the local polls.
The coalition last week had threatened to boycott the election but relented when authorities appointed their representatives to the commissions.

A team of election observers from the United States and several other states from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) were monitoring voting at some of the 10,000 polling stations.
During the campaign, opposition leaders were virtually shut out from state media and could only reach voters through rallies and a handful of independent papers.

"This election is not fair but we have no choice. We must accept to fight under such conditions," Vuk Draskovic, leader of the biggest party in the coalition, the Serbian Renewal Movement, told reporters.
Voters queuing at polling stations voiced only bitterness about an election which they believed would change nothing.

"We will live like this all our lives if these people remain in power," said Dragan, 40, an electrician with an unemployed wife and teenage daughter. "With these authorities, there can be no revival of the economy or progress."
The low turnout testified to the widespread apathy among the population of which almost a third now lives in poverty, according to a Red Cross survey.
A year of peace and the end of a U.N. trade embargo has failed to bring economic relief to a country which once enjoyed the highest standard of living in Eastern Europe.
The opposition coalition has tried to capitalise on widespread discontent over the troubled economy. But the coalition was hampered by the state media blockade and by divisions within its own ranks.

Although Milosevic is not a candidate in the polls, an election victory for his parties should enable him to push through constitutional change enabling him to stay in power after his second and final term as president expires next year.
Diplomats say he will probably assume the post of federal president after the next federal parliament invests the ceremonial post with strong executive authority.
Official results were not due before Thursday but unofficial returns early in the week were likely to indicate the outcome.
